live.name: SmokeLoader
live.headline: SmokeLoader: a loader first revealed in 2011, now seen hiding in concatenated ZIP files
live.in_short: SmokeLoader is a loader that can act as a keylogger, stealer, botnet or backdoor. Perception Point links a 2024 phishing attack using a concatenated ZIP disguised as a shipping document to it.

sentences.t: SmokeLoader is a malware family of the loader type, and one source says it was first revealed in 2011.
The same source says it is a family that keeps evolving and aims to work as a keylogger, information stealer, botnet or backdoor.
The cards name no specific group behind it. Perception Point refers only to unnamed threat actors who distributed the malware in a recent attack.
SmokeLoader is spread through emails and drive-by downloads, according to one technical analysis.
The same analysis says it was the first to use PROPagate injection, a way of running code inside a different application from the one that is running.
Perception Point describes a phishing email sent under the guise of a shipping company. The attackers changed the file name and extension so the attachment looked like a RAR archive.
The file was a concatenated ZIP. Perception Point says opening it in 7zip shows only a benign-looking PDF, while WinRAR reads the second central directory and shows the second archive.
The hidden item was an AutoIt-based executable. The report says Windows File Explorer struggles with concatenated ZIPs and may fail to open the file at all.
Perception Point says 7zip may show a warning about extra data after the archive end, but that it is easily overlooked. It also says 7zip's developers consider the behaviour intentional.
In a blog post dated 2024-11-07, Perception Point linked the attack path it analysed to SmokeLoader.
The report describes the executable as a variant of a trojan family. It says the eventual payload could include banking trojans or ransomware.
The tests used 7zip 22.01, WinRAR 7.01 and Windows 23H2. The report says the techniques apply to the latest versions of these tools as of its date.
Treat unexpected shipping documents with caution, even when the file looks like a plain archive or PDF.
Do not rely on a single archive tool to show what a file contains.
